hmmt-feb-2016-alg-02.title: Factor when $n$ has an odd divisor
hmmt-feb-2016-alg-02.body:
$n=1,2,4$ give $2,5,257$, all prime.

If $n>1$ is odd, $n^n+1$ is even and larger than $2$. If $n$ is even and has an odd divisor $m>1$, then $n^n+1=(n^{n/m})^m+1$ is divisible by $n^{n/m}+1$, which is strictly between $1$ and $n^n+1$, so it is composite. The remaining even $n$ in range are powers of two: $n=2,4,8$ ($16>15$); $n=8$ gives $2^{24}+1=(2^8)^3+1$, divisible by $2^8+1$, so composite.

**Answer: $n=1,2,4$**

hmmt-feb-2016-alg-03.title: Write the elements as $10^i+10^j$
hmmt-feb-2016-alg-03.body:
The elements of $A$ are $10^i+10^j$ with $0\le i\le j\le3$ (for $i=j$ this is $2\cdot10^i$). The sum over $i\le j$ equals $\frac12\left[\sum_{i,j}(10^i+10^j)^2+\sum_i(2\cdot10^i)^2\right]$. With $S_2=\sum_{i=0}^310^{2i}=1010101$ and $S_1=\sum_{i=0}^310^i=1111$: $\sum_{i,j}(10^i+10^j)^2=2\cdot4S_2+2S_1^2=8080808+2468642=10549450$ and $\sum(2\cdot10^i)^2=4S_2=4040404$. So the answer is $\frac{10549450+4040404}2=7294927$.

**Answer: 7294927**

hmmt-feb-2016-alg-04.title: Remove the fractional parts
hmmt-feb-2016-alg-04.body:
Let $r_i=2^i\bmod25$. Then $\left\lfloor\frac{2^i}{25}\right\rfloor=\frac{2^i-r_i}{25}$, so the sum is $\frac{(2^{2016}-1)-\sum_{i=0}^{2015}r_i}{25}$. The order of $2$ mod $25$ is $20$, and over one period the $r_i$ are the residues $1,\ldots,24$ other than $5,10,15,20$, summing to $300-50=250$. As $2016=100\cdot20+16$ and $\sum_{i=0}^{15}r_i=185$, we get $\sum r_i=25000+185=25185$. So the sum equals $\frac{2^{2016}-25186}{25}$, and we need $2^{2016}-25186\pmod{2500}$.

Modulo $4$: $2^{2016}\equiv0$. Modulo $625$: $\varphi(625)=500$, so $2^{2016}\equiv2^{16}=65536\equiv536$. By CRT $2^{2016}\equiv536\pmod{2500}$ ($536\equiv0\pmod4$). Hence $2^{2016}-25186\equiv536-25186\equiv350\pmod{2500}$, and dividing by $25$ gives $14\pmod{100}$.

**Answer: 14**

hmmt-feb-2016-alg-05.title: A closed form for partial sums
hmmt-feb-2016-alg-05.body:
Claim: $S_n=a_1+\cdots+a_n=2a_1+a_3+a_{n-1}-a_{n-2}$ for $n\ge3$. For $n=3$: $2a_1+a_3+a_2-a_1=a_1+a_2+a_3$ ✓. If it holds for $n$, then $S_{n+1}-S_n$ by the formula equals $(a_n-a_{n-1})-(a_{n-1}-a_{n-2})=a_n-2a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}=a_{n+1}$ by the recurrence (with index shifted), as required.

With $n=100$: $S_{100}=2\cdot1+1+a_{99}-a_{98}=3$.

**Answer: 3**

hmmt-feb-2016-alg-06.title: Even versus odd
hmmt-feb-2016-alg-06.body:
**Even $N>2$ is not special.** Numbers coprime to $N$ are odd, and for $k=3$ a sum of three odd numbers is odd, so it cannot equal $N$. **$N=2$ is special**: $k=2$, $2=1+1$.

**Odd $N\ge3$ is special.** Powers of $2$ are coprime to $N$. Writing $N$ in binary shows $N$ is a sum of exactly $k$ powers of $2$ for every $k$ with $\mathrm{popcount}(N)\le k\le N$ (split a power $2^m>1$ into two copies of $2^{m-1}$ repeatedly). For smaller $k\ge2$: let $2^a<N$ be the largest power of $2$ below $N$; then $\gcd(N-2^a,N)=\gcd(2^a,N)=1$, and splitting $2^a$ into $k-1$ powers of $2$ ($1\le k-1\le 2^a$) gives $N$ as a sum of $k$ terms coprime to $N$, for $2\le k\le2^a+1$. Since $\mathrm{popcount}(N)\le a+1\le2^a+1$, the two ranges together cover every $k$ from $2$ to $N$.

So the special integers below $100$ are $2$ and the $49$ odd numbers $3,5,\ldots,99$: $50$ in all.

**Answer: 50**

hmmt-feb-2016-alg-07.title: 2-adic valuation of $A-2^{10n}$
hmmt-feb-2016-alg-07.body:
For $j\le16$, $1024^j=1.024^j\cdot10^{3j}$ with $1\le1.024^j<10$, so $2^{10j}$ has exactly $3j+1$ digits. For $n\le16$, concatenation gives $A=\sum_{i=1}^n2^{10i}\cdot10^{D_i}$ with $D_i=\sum_{j=i+1}^n(3j+1)$, so $$A-2^{10n}=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}2^{10i+D_i}\,5^{D_i},$$ and the $i$-th term has $2$-adic valuation $u_i=10i+D_i$. Then $u_i-u_{i-1}=10-(3i+1)=3(3-i)$, so $u_i$ increases up to $i=3$ and decreases afterwards: the minimum is at $i=1$ or $i=n-1$, with $u_{n-1}=13n-9$ and $u_1=\frac{3n^2+5n+12}2$.

We need $v_2(A-2^{10n})\ge170$. If the minimum valuation is attained by a unique term, it equals $v_2(A-2^{10n})$, so we need $13n-9\ge170$, i.e. $n\ge14$ (and $u_1$ is huge). The only tie in $3\le n\le16$ is $n=5$ ($u_1=u_4=56$), where the sum of the two terms has valuation at most $57$ (a direct check), far below $170$. For $n=14$: $u_{13}=173$ and all other $u_i\ge173$, so $2^{170}\mid A-2^{140}$. Hence the smallest $n$ is $14$.

**Answer: 14**

hmmt-feb-2016-alg-08.title: Product of the units mod $n$
hmmt-feb-2016-alg-08.body:
$\phi^!(n)$ is (the residue of) the product of all elements of the unit group $U(n)$. Pair each unit with its inverse; the product is $1$ for pairs $u\ne u^{-1}$, so $\phi^!(n)\equiv\prod_{u^2=1}u$, the product of the elements of order $\le2$. These come in pairs $\{u,-u\}$ with product $-u^2=-1$ (for $n>2$, $u\ne-u$), so the product is $(-1)^{m/2}$ where $m$ is the number of solutions of $u^2\equiv1$. Here $m$ is a power of $2$ (it is the number of elements of order at most $2$ in the abelian group $U(n)$), so the product is $-1$ iff $m=2$, iff $U(n)$ has a unique element of order $2$ (is cyclic), i.e. $n\in\{4,p^k,2p^k\}$ with $p$ an odd prime. Also $n=2$ works ($\phi^!(2)+1=2$).

Counting in $[2,50]$: $n=2,4$ ($2$ numbers); odd prime powers $\le50$: $14$ primes and $9,25,27,49$ ($18$ numbers); $2p^k\le50$, i.e. $p^k\le25$: $3,5,7,11,13,17,19,23,9,25$ ($10$ numbers). Total $2+18+10=30$.

**Answer: 30**

hmmt-feb-2016-alg-09.title: A circulant determinant
hmmt-feb-2016-alg-09.body:
Since $(-1)^{f(\pi)}=\operatorname{sgn}\pi$, the generating function $F(x)=\sum_{\pi\in S_n}(-1)^{f(\pi)}x^{g(\pi)}$ equals $\det A_n(x)$, where $A_n(x)$ is the $n\times n$ matrix with entry $x$ at positions $(i,j)$ with $j\equiv i\pm1\pmod n$ and $1$ elsewhere. We want $F(-1)$.

$A_n(x)=J+(x-1)(Z+Z^{-1})$ with $J$ the all-ones matrix and $Z$ the cyclic shift. The eigenvector $(1,\ldots,1)$ has eigenvalue $n+2(x-1)=2x+n-2$; for $\omega=e^{2\pi ij/n}$ ($1\le j\le n-1$), $J$ contributes $0$ and the eigenvalue is $(x-1)(\omega+\omega^{-1})$. Hence $$F(x)=(2x+n-2)(x-1)^{n-1}\prod_{j=1}^{n-1}2\cos\frac{2\pi j}n.$$ For odd $n$, $\prod_{j=1}^{n-1}(\omega^j+\omega^{-j})=\omega^{-n(n-1)/2}\prod_{j=1}^{n-1}(1+\omega^{2j})=\prod_{k=1}^{n-1}(1+\omega^k)$, because $n(n-1)/2$ is a multiple of $n$ and $2j$ runs over all nonzero residues. Finally $\prod_{k=1}^{n-1}(x-\omega^k)=1+x+\cdots+x^{n-1}$ equals $1$ at $x=-1$ ($n$ odd), so $\prod(1+\omega^k)=(-1)^{n-1}\cdot1=1$. So $F(x)=(2x+n-2)(x-1)^{n-1}$ and $$F(-1)=(n-4)(-2)^{n-1}=995\cdot2^{998}\quad(n=999).$$

**Answer: $995\cdot2^{998}$**

hmmt-feb-2016-alg-10.title: Fermat point and an inversion
hmmt-feb-2016-alg-10.body:
Take a point $P$ and rays $PA,PB,PC$ with $\angle APB=\angle BPC=\angle CPA=120^\circ$ and $PA=a$, $PB=b$, $PC=c$. By the law of cosines, $AB^2=a^2+ab+b^2=9$, $BC^2=52$, $CA^2=49$, so $AB=3$, $BC=2\sqrt{13}$, $CA=7$. Then $\cos\angle BAC=\frac{9+49-52}{2\cdot3\cdot7}=\frac17$ and $\sin\angle BAC=\frac{4\sqrt3}7$.

Invert about $A$ with radius $\rho$, denoting images by primes. Since inversion preserves $\angle APB\to\angle AB'P'$, we get $\angle AB'P'=\angle AC'P'=120^\circ$, so in the quadrilateral $AB'P'C'$, $\angle B'P'C'=360^\circ-240^\circ-\angle A=120^\circ-\angle A$, with $\cos(120^\circ-A)=-\frac12\cdot\frac17+\frac{\sqrt3}2\cdot\frac{4\sqrt3}7=\frac{11}{14}$. Using $X'Y'=\frac{\rho^2XY}{AX\cdot AY}$: $B'P'=\frac{\rho^2b}{3a}$, $P'C'=\frac{\rho^2c}{7a}$, $B'C'=\frac{\rho^2\cdot2\sqrt{13}}{21}$. The law of cosines in $\triangle B'P'C'$ gives $$\frac{52}{441}=\frac{b^2}{9a^2}+\frac{c^2}{49a^2}-2\cdot\frac{bc}{21a^2}\cdot\frac{11}{14},$$ i.e. $52=\dfrac{49b^2+9c^2-33bc}{a^2}$.

**Answer: 52**
